ramen.title: Ramen
lines: Take a mouthful of broth with the flat spoon (renge, れんげ) first, then go to the noodles and taste how the two work together.
Slurping is not a breach. If you would rather not make the noise, lay the noodles into the renge and eat from that — it also stops the broth spitting.
🔴 You do not have to finish the broth. Draining the bowl reads as a compliment to whoever made it, but leaving it is not read as one either way — so drink what you want of it and stop.

tsukemen.title: Tsukemen — dipping noodles
lines: Two bowls: cold noodles in one, thick hot broth in the other. ⚠ The broth is a dip and is never poured over the noodles.
🔴 Two or three strands at a time, dipped briefly rather than soaked. A whole clump cools the broth and it does not recover.
The spring onion, menma and chāshū on the noodle plate can go through the broth or be eaten straight — either is normal.
🔴 When the noodles are gone, ask for soup-wari (スープ割り). Hot dashi is poured into the dip that is left so the thick broth thins into something you can drink. It is the closing step, not an extra.

shirunashi-tantanmen.title: Soupless dandan noodles
lines: 🔴 It arrives unfinished. Mix it — the Hiroshima figure is thirty turns or more, and the shop’s own line is simply that the harder you mix it the better it gets. Under-mixing is how this dish disappoints.
Heat is a number and nothing else: 1辛 to 4辛 is 10 ml to 40 ml of chilli oil in the same bowl.
The huājiāo / sanshō on the table goes on at the end, to taste.
If a soft-boiled egg comes alongside, the local way is to dip the noodles into it like sukiyaki — it takes the edge off the chilli.
When the noodles are gone, ask for oimeshi (追い飯): rice tipped into the tare left in the bowl, with a splash of soy and, if you want it, vinegar.

soba-udon.title: Soba and udon
lines: 🔴 Cold (zaru / mori): dip about the last third of the strands into the tsuyu. Sinking the whole bundle drowns the flour flavour the shop is selling.
Put the wasabi and the other yakumi ON the noodles and dip that, rather than stirring them into the tsuyu — dissolved, the wasabi loses its edge.
Draw the mouthful up in one go. The air is what carries the smell.

🔴 At a SOBA shop — not a udon one — a jug of cloudy soba-yu (そば湯), the water the noodles were boiled in, comes out at the end. Swirl it first, because the good part settles, then pour it into what is left of your tsuyu and drink that.

okonomiyaki-hiroshima.title: Hiroshima okonomiyaki
lines: It is built in layers, not stirred, and it is slid onto the hot steel in front of you rather than onto a plate.
🔴 The small metal spatula (hera / kote, へら・こて) is the cutlery. Push a corner of the blade in at about 45°, then bring it upright to cut through.
Cut it in a grid into squares of about 2–3 cm. Pie wedges look right and eat badly. Then carry each square to your mouth on the corner of the blade.

⚠ Rest the hot spatula with only its tip on the rim of the griddle. Laid ACROSS the exhaust slot the heat runs up the handle and the handle burns you — shops post signs about it, and it has melted menus.
Eating it off a plate with chopsticks is explicitly fine; shops say a first-timer may as well start there.

okonomiyaki-kyoto.title: Kyoto beta-yaki
lines: Kyoto’s own style: the batter is spread thin and the fillings — cabbage, pork, seafood — are piled on top rather than mixed through it.
Sauce, and then mayonnaise, aonori and katsuobushi over that, is the standard finish.
🔴 Eat it straight off the griddle while it is still fierce. This one is built around being eaten hot, and it does not survive being left.

sukiyaki-shabushabu.title: Sukiyaki and shabu-shabu
sukiyaki-shabushabu.title_jp: すき焼き・しゃぶしゃぶ
lines: 🔴 Kansai sukiyaki uses no pre-mixed sauce. Sugar, sake and soy go straight into the pot over the meat — there is no jug of warishita to pour, which is the Kantō way and not this one.
Beat the raw egg in your small bowl and dip each piece into it as it comes out.
Shabu-shabu: the slow things go in first — spring onion, daikon, tofu — and once the pot is back to the boil you take the meat a slice at a time and swim it in the broth.
🔴 Beef and seafood are ready the moment the colour begins to change, still half-raw in the middle. Pork is the exception and wants cooking through.
Ponzu or sesame sauce for dipping. The shime (〆) at the end is rice or noodles dropped into the broth everything has cooked in.

chanko-nabe.title: Chanko nabe
lines: Chicken, cabbage, carrot, spring onion, tofu and fried tofu simmered in a chicken-bone or dashi broth.
🔴 It is not ready when it lands. The slowest things go in first, and you eat each one as it comes good rather than waiting for the pot.
The shime: bring what is left of the broth back to the boil, add a little water, stir loosened rice in, and pour beaten egg over it — off the heat as soon as the egg just sets. That is zōsui (雑炊).

tonkatsu.title: Tonkatsu
lines: 🔴 If a small ridged mortar of sesame seeds arrives, that is the sauce dish. Grind the seeds first — about five to seven turns, leaving them half whole; ground to powder the aroma goes.
Then pour the sauce into the mortar and dip each piece of cutlet in it. The bottle is not for pouring over the pork.
Karashi mustard goes onto the cutlet first, and that piece then goes into the sesame sauce.

kamameshi.title: Kamameshi
lines: 🔴 Serve into the bowl with the paddle and shut the wooden lid again every single time. Left open, the rice stops steaming, goes hard, and the crust welds itself to the pot.
If yakumi and chopped pickles come with it, the shop’s own order is four passes: plain first, then with the yakumi, then with the pickles, then dashi or tea poured over the last bowlful as ochazuke.
The scorched crust on the bottom (okoge, おこげ) is what the pot is for — it lifts cleanly once the rice has steamed properly.
⚠ The pot is extremely hot. Hold it steady through the damp towel, not with a bare hand.

ekiben.title: Ekiben — station boxes
lines: 🔴 Station boxes are made low-smell on purpose, because they get opened next to a stranger. If you buy food elsewhere to eat on the train, apply the same test.
Eat it soon after boarding rather than saving it — that is the easiest window for everyone around you.
Bins are in the deck by the doors and on the platform. ⚠ Nothing gets left under the seat.

kakinoha-zushi.title: Kakinoha-zushi — persimmon-leaf sushi
lines: 🔴 The leaf is a wrapper and it is not eaten. It is there to keep the rice from drying and to preserve it — the antibacterial effect was only worked out later.
Peel from the BACK, and only down one side, the way you open a banana. The sushi comes up out of the leaf and the leaf stays as a handle, so your fingers stay clean.
⚑ The maker puts the right temperature for the rice at about 20 °C. Straight out of a fridge it goes hard — in cold weather they suggest a few seconds of microwave rather than eating it chilled.

teishoku.title: Set meals
lines: Rice, soup, a main and small sides land together. The order is soup first, then rice, then the dishes.
🔴 Small bowls and little sauce dishes are picked up in your hand. The big plates — grilled fish, sashimi, tempura — stay on the table.
A lidded bowl is opened by tracing a の along the rim, so the condensation on the underside runs back into the bowl and not onto the tray.
⚠ Don’t stack the plates when you finish. It reads as tidying up after the kitchen.

curry-rice.title: Japanese curry-rice
lines: A spoon comes with it and nothing else.

🔴 The two things at the side of the plate do different jobs. The red shreds (fukujinzuke, 福神漬) are sweet, and that sweetness lifts the spice. The pickled shallots (rakkyō, らっきょう) are sweet-sour and reset the mouth between spoonfuls.
Take them a little at a time as you go, rather than clearing them at the start or leaving them.

spice-curry.title: Spice curry
lines: Several sauces, the rice and small sharp pickled sides arrive on one plate, kept apart.
🔴 Mix a LITTLE at a time — a bit of one sauce, a bit of rice, a bit of pickle — rather than stirring the whole plate together at the start. Each spoonful is meant to be a different combination.
The pickles (achar, アチャール) are there to add sharpness and depth to the milder parts of the plate, not as decoration.

grilled-oysters.title: Grilled oysters
lines: 🔴 They are cooked in the CLOSED shell, so they steam in their own liquor and arrive shut. Open them over the plate — the liquid inside is boiling and it is also the seasoning, so it does not get tipped away.
They come in twos rather than by the dozen. Both Miyajima houses on this trip are sit-down restaurants with tables, not standing stalls.

⚠ Outside on the arcade the deer will eat anything a person eats, and paper too. Feeding them is banned by the prefecture and the city, and the standing request is to feed nothing and carry your rubbish off the island.

yudofu-yuba.title: Yudōfu
lines: The pot is kombu dashi, not plain water — kombu steeped for fifteen to thirty minutes before it ever goes on the flame.
🔴 The tofu is ready as soon as it is hot through. Don’t let it boil: over-cooked it goes rubbery, and that is the one thing that spoils this dish.
Lift it out into your own bowl and dip it in the tare — ponzu, or a dashi-soy — and build the yakumi yourself: chopped spring onion, grated ginger, a wedge of sudachi to squeeze over.

donburi.title: Shirasu and rice bowls
lines: Whitebait over vinegared or plain rice, with soy trickled over the top. Nori, shiso, chopped spring onion or an egg yolk go on as well; noodle tsuyu, ponzu or ginger-soy are the usual alternatives to plain soy.
🔴 Raw and boiled are different dishes, not different grades. Nama-shirasu (生しらす) is untreated; kama-age (釜揚げ) is boiled; shirasu-boshi is boiled then sun-dried.

⚑ Raw whitebait goes off fast enough that it can only be eaten on the day it is landed, so whether it is on the board is a question about this morning’s boats. The season runs 11 March to 31 December, so late October is inside it.

bought-food.title: Bought food — konbini, bento chains, supermarkets
lines: 🔴 At the till you are asked whether you are eating in. That question is not small talk: the shop sets the tax from your answer at the moment of sale — 10% eating in, 8% taking away — and it does not change afterwards whatever you then do. Say takeaway and take it away.
You will also be asked "atatamemasu ka?" (温めますか？) — shall I heat it? Hai (はい) yes, daijōbu desu (だいじょうぶです) no. Chopsticks are asked about separately and handed over at the counter.

🔴 Supermarket discount stickers come in three waves: around 16:00–17:00 at 10–20% off, around 19:00–20:00 at 20–30%, and from one to two hours before closing at 30% down to half price. Bento, lunch plates and sushi get an extra pass at about 14:00–16:00.
⚑ The wave starts EARLY when rain is forecast, because the customers come early too.
⚠ There are almost no bins on Japanese streets. The bin is beside the shop counter or its door — use it before you walk out, or the packaging comes back to the hotel with you.

quick.intro: Not every night ends in a restaurant. These are the places near each base that are still open when a day runs late, checked against their operators’ own pages. Read the closing time, not the distance — and for how the till works, what the two questions mean and when the discount stickers go on, open 🏪 Bought food in the "How each dish is eaten" card just below.

bases.title: Tokyo — Akihabara
bases.note: 🔴 The late answer here is Yoshinoya, 250 m up Shōwa-dōri and open to 02:00 — nothing else in this list is open past midnight. For a cold box, Life runs to 24:00, and the deepest discounts land one to two hours before a store closes: at this one that is roughly 22:00–23:00, which is exactly when a long day gets back.

options.what: Cooked-to-order hot bento — karaage, ginger pork, katsu-don. No seating; it is made while you wait, so allow ten minutes.

options.note: ⚠ The address the chain publishes stops at the block number, so the pin is approximate. Listed for the 24-hour opening rather than for the food.

options.name_jp: デニーズ 秋葉原中央口店
options.hours: ⚠ UNVERIFIED — Denny’s own store page leaves the hours field blank, and third-party listings split between 24 hours and 06:30–23:00. Treat it as a look-on-the-way-past, not a plan.

options.what: Sit-down family restaurant: rice plates, pasta, breakfast sets, drink bar.

options.note: ⚑ It is one floor below your room, which is why it is here despite the unverified hours — worth a glance on the way in on the first night, and then you know.

bases.title: Kyoto — Kyoto Station
bases.note: 🔴 The Kyoto base answers this question in the lobby: the Dormy Inn serves a free bowl of ramen every night, 21:30–23:00, which lands on top of every late return from Nara and Yoshino. ⛔ There is no Hotto Motto near Kyoto Station and no Fresco within a comfortable walk — that was checked against both operators’ own store lists, not assumed. ⚠ The supermarket and the 24-hour Yoshinoya are both on the Hachijō (south) side, so add the walk through or under the station.

options.what: A small bowl of light shōyu ramen, free to guests. Also on the house: ice lollies on 9F 15:00–01:00, and a lactic drink 9F 05:00–10:00. The bath runs 15:00–10:00; breakfast 06:30–09:30, last entry 09:00.
options.note: 🔴 This is the single most useful fact for late nights on the trip: ten of the twenty nights are here, and 21:30 is after almost every last train back from Nara. ⚠ No in-room or floor microwave is confirmed — the hotel’s own floor plan lists only 9F laundry and vending on 2F/5F/9F — so do not count on reheating a cold supermarket box here.

options.hours: Omiyage Kaidō 07:30–22:00 · Porta Dining 11:00–22:00 · B1 café 07:00–23:00 · drugstore 07:00–22:00

options.walk: ≈835 m straight line — Hachijō side, so allow 15 minutes through the station
options.what: A full supermarket on the ground floor of the Aeon Mall, with the prepared-food and bento counters a Japanese supermarket normally has.
options.address_jp: 京都市南区西九条鳥居口町1 イオンモールKYOTO 1F
options.note: ⚠ The one real supermarket near this base, and it is on the wrong side of the station. Closing at 22:00 puts the deepest discount wave at roughly 20:00–21:00. Pin is the mall.

options.name_jp: 吉野家 京都八条口店
options.what: Beef bowls, table seating, takeaway, and it never closes.
options.address_jp: 〒601-8411 京都府京都市南区西九条北ノ内町41-4
options.note: ⚑ The fallback if a night runs past 23:00 and the free ramen has finished. Pin geocoded from the address.

bases.title: Hiroshima — Hiroshima Station
bases.note: Everything here is inside the station buildings, three to five minutes from the hotel door, and the whole cluster shuts between 22:00 and 22:30 — ⛔ after that there is nothing but konbini. ⚠ Miyajima day (8 Nov) is the one to watch: be back across the tracks by 22:00 or the plan is a convenience store. There is no Hotto Motto and no Fresta near this station; both were checked against the operators’ own lists.

options.walk: ≈375 m — ekie 1F, inside the station building
options.what: A proper supermarket inside the station, weighted towards ready-to-eat: bento, prepared dishes, local products.
options.address_jp: 〒732-0822 広島県広島市南区松原町1-2 ekie 1F
options.note: 🔴 The default for both Hiroshima nights, and the base where a cold box actually works — ⚑ the Sotetsu Fresa is the one hotel of the three whose own site lists a microwave. Closing at 22:00 puts the deepest discount wave at roughly 20:00–21:00. Pin is the station building.

options.walk: ≈375 m — ekie 1F, same floor as Yours
options.what: A row of takeaway counters beside the supermarket: Kuroben, NUMBER 8, Green gourmet and others selling boxed meals and prepared dishes.
options.note: ⚠ Individual counter hours are not published on the floor guide, so treat the floor’s 22:00 as the ceiling and expect some shutters down earlier. Named so you know what is there, not as something to rely on at 21:45.

options.name_jp: 吉野家 広島駅北口店
options.what: Beef bowls with table seating, plus takeaway. The latest-closing hot food in the station.
options.address_jp: 〒732-0822 広島県広島市南区松原町1-2 ekie 1F
options.note: ⚑ 22:30 is the last hot meal at this base. Pin is the station building.

options.name_jp: 吉野家 ミナモア広島店

options.what: Same menu, takeaway and pre-order from the phone; the nearest of the two branches.
options.address_jp: 〒732-0822 広島県広島市南区松原町2-37 ミナモア広島
options.note: ⚠ Last order 21:30, half an hour before the ekie branch stops serving. Closer, but it closes first. Pin is the building.

bases.title: Day hubs — buying a lunch to carry
bases.note: 🔴 The rule these two set is the same one: buy the carried lunch at the hub you pass through, not at the place you are going. Nara has a konbini inside the gates; Yoshino has nothing at the station at all.

options.name_en: FamilyMart Kintetsu Nara Station (inside the gates)

options.address_jp: 奈良県奈良市東向中町29
options.note: ⚑ Being inside the gates is the whole point: it costs no detour on days 8, 9 and 10. Pin omitted — it is a unit on a station concourse and a coordinate would resolve to the building either way.

options.kind: ⛔ there is nothing here — listed so you do not go looking

gaps: ⛔ Hotto Motto reaches only the Tokyo base. The nearest branch to Kyoto Station is Nishi-Ōji-Shichijō, and to Hiroshima Station it is Midori 3-chōme — both far enough out to be pointless. Checked against the chain’s own city lists on 2026-08-22.
⛔ No supermarket sits on the Dormy Inn’s own side of Kyoto Station. Fresco’s nearest 24-hour branch (Gojō) is about 1.2 km. The free 21:30 ramen downstairs is what replaces it.

⚠ Microwaves: only the Sotetsu Fresa in Hiroshima lists one on its own site. Akihabara Washington publishes a 3F coin laundry and nothing else; the Dormy Inn publishes 9F laundry and vending on 2F/5F/9F, and a third-party listing claiming service corners on floors 2–8 is not confirmed by the hotel. ⇒ At the Tokyo and Kyoto bases, assume a cold box stays cold.

⚠ Only two day hubs were researched — Nara and Yoshino, the two where the answer changes what you do. Kamakura, Takaosanguchi, Uji and Miyajimaguchi are unchecked; say the word and they get the same treatment.

mendokoro-honda.order_how: 🔴 Ticket machine, and the rule is not the obvious one. The machine stands OUTSIDE the shop, but you do NOT buy first — signs on the wall ask you to join the back of the queue with no ticket. A member of staff comes down the line and asks whether you have bought one; that is your cue to step out, buy, and return to your place. The machine takes cards, Suica and QR.
mendokoro-honda.order: Shōyu ramen — the flagship bowl. A tare blended from five soy sauces over a broth drawn from chicken, pork, dried sardine and clam, with thin noodles cut in-house from three Japanese wheat flours.
mendokoro-honda.order_jp: 醤油ラーメンを ひとつ お願いします
mendokoro-honda.order_romaji: Shōyu rāmen o hitotsu onegai shimasu
mendokoro-honda.order_why: The Chiyoda tourism board and the shop's own reputation both put this bowl first — it is the one the place is built on. The machine offers five bases (shōyu, shōyu tsukemen, shio, shio tsukemen, and a soupless tantanmen); the plain shōyu button is the one to press on a first visit.
mendokoro-honda.order_backup: If you want it richer, tokusei shōyu ramen (特製醤油ラーメン) is the same bowl with seven slices of chāshū, a soft-boiled marinated egg and better nori. ⚑ The shop's other draw, shio tsukemen (塩つけ麺), is cold noodles served sitting in kombu water, with seaweed salt and a sudachi lime alongside to season them before they go into the broth — a summer order, and all three of the evenings you might be here are late October or November, so it is named for completeness rather than recommended.

kamayoshi.order_how: Order at the counter — staff take it, no ticket machine. Cards, Suica and QR are all accepted. Fourteen seats and no reservations. ⚠ Two things the shop asks in writing: it has no storage, so do not arrive with the trolley — leave luggage at the hotel first; and at weekday lunch it asks you to free the table 20–30 minutes after eating. Neither applies if you go at dinner.
kamayoshi.order: Gobō-ten udon — burdock in tempura batter, fried fresh and laid across the noodles in big pieces.
kamayoshi.order_jp: ごぼう天うどんを ひとつ お願いします
kamayoshi.order_romaji: Gobō-ten udon o hitotsu onegai shimasu
kamayoshi.order_why: The hybrid comes from the owner: he is from Fukuoka, so the dashi is Hakata — flying fish with kombu and katsuo — while the noodles are Sanuki, thick and hard-chewed, made in-house from Kagawa wheat. Burdock tempura is one of the two toppings Fukuoka's own tourism office names as the standard on a Hakata bowl, which is what makes this the bowl that shows what the shop is doing. ⚑ Worth knowing before you order: the bowl reported as the shop's own best-seller is not this one — it is tori-chikuwa-ten udon (とりちくわ天うどん), chicken and fishcake tempura together, and that tempura is fried after the order goes in.
kamayoshi.order_backup: Niku udon (肉うどん) is the beef bowl, and every bowl here is offered hot or cold. The three Special sets stack the tempura instead of choosing between them — A is four kinds (chicken, chikuwa, aubergine, maitake), B is three with beef and a hot-spring egg, C is five with beef.

tonkatsu-marugo.order_how: 🔴 CASH ONLY — no cards, no IC, no QR. Bring notes. Table service, no reservations. ⚑ The queue here is a lunch phenomenon, not an evening one — reports put about 29 people waiting for the 11:30 lunch opening against two at 16:50 for the 17:00 dinner opening, so arrive at the open and it costs ten minutes rather than forty. Adding the set (定食) for a few hundred yen turns the cutlet into a meal with rice, pickles and red-miso soup, and the rice and cabbage are then refillable free.
tonkatsu-marugo.order: Toku-rōsu katsu — the premium loin cutlet, thick-cut, with a fat edge left on.
tonkatsu-marugo.order_jp: 特ロースかつ定食を ひとつ お願いします
tonkatsu-marugo.order_romaji: Toku-rōsu katsu teishoku o hitotsu onegai shimasu
tonkatsu-marugo.order_why: The shop has been frying since 1975 on Yamagata sangen-ton pork, and the two cutlets it is judged on are the premium loin and the premium fillet. The loin is the fattier and the more talked-about of the two. ⚑ The shop's Tonkatsu Hyakumeiten standing, 2026 being the current selection, is awarded to the shop and not to either cut.
tonkatsu-marugo.order_backup: Toku-hire katsu (特ヒレかつ) is the same cooking on the lean fillet — no fat edge, a little more money, and the choice if you would rather not chew through pork fat at the end of a long day.

ponta-honke.order_how: Table service across three floors; the ground floor is a three-seat counter and the rest is upstairs. Cards are accepted. ⚠ Reservations are taken only for two or more, so on your own it is walk-in — go early rather than late. Closed Mondays.
ponta-honke.order: Katsuretsu — the trimmed core of the loin, every scrap of fat cut away, cooked in house-rendered lard at low temperature, closer to a French côtelette than to modern tonkatsu.
ponta-honke.order_jp: カツレツを ひとつ お願いします
ponta-honke.order_why: This is where the dish comes from. The house opened in 1905 under a founder who had cooked Western food in the Imperial Household kitchen, and its katsuretsu is the ancestor that later became tonkatsu everywhere else — over ten minutes in low lard, then a moment in hot, and served without the heavy sauce. Ordering anything else here is ordering around the reason to come.
ponta-honke.order_backup: The stews are the other half of the house — tan-shichū (タンシチュー), the tongue stew the shop itself puts forward, and a beef stew beside it. ⚠ Both cost getting on for double the cutlet. In late October and November the fried oysters (カキフライ) are in season, which is the one time of year they beat all of it.

delhi-ueno.order_how: 🔴 CASH ONLY — no cards, no e-money. Fifteen seats, counter and small tables, no reservations, and it runs straight through from late morning to half nine, so an awkward hour is fine here.
delhi-ueno.order: Kashmir curry — jet-black, soup-thin, poured over rice. Very hot, and hot in a clean way rather than a blunt one.
delhi-ueno.order_jp: カシミールカレーを ひとつ お願いします
delhi-ueno.order_romaji: Kashmīru karē o hitotsu onegai shimasu
delhi-ueno.order_why: The shop has been on this corner since 1956 and this is the curry it is famous for; its own menu marks it five chillies out of five, the top of the shop's scale. It is thin enough to drink and much hotter than it looks, which is the whole point of the dish.
delhi-ueno.order_backup: ⚠ If the top of the scale is not what you want after a long day, go down it by name, not by guess: Delhi curry (デリーカレー) is the mild one at one chilli, Indo curry (インドカレー) the thicker, more conventional middle at three.

gonokami-seisakusho.order_how: 🔴 Ticket machine, and 🔴 CASH ONLY. The machine is INSIDE, and what you do depends on whether there is a line: if the pavement outside is clear, walk in and buy at the machine; if people are waiting on the street, join the end and let staff call you in — do not walk past a line to the machine. ⚑ At the hour this day arrives there is usually no line. ⚑ When you hand the ticket over you are asked one question: nami-mori or ko-mori (並盛 / 小盛), regular or small portion. Say 'nami-mori' for regular.
gonokami-seisakusho.order: Ebi tsukemen — cold noodles you dip into a hot, almost sauce-thick soup made from a large quantity of sweet shrimp.
gonokami-seisakusho.order_jp: 海老つけ麺を ひとつ お願いします
gonokami-seisakusho.order_romaji: Ebi tsukemen o hitotsu onegai shimasu
gonokami-seisakusho.order_why: The shop is built around prawn tsukemen and this is the base bowl the other versions are built on. Under the shrimp is a pork- and chicken-bone stock with mackerel and dried sardine in it, and the shrimp is what gives the broth the body that coats the noodles instead of running off them.
gonokami-seisakusho.order_backup: Ebi tomato tsukemen (海老トマトつけ麺) turns the same broth sharper and is the one regulars switch to; ebi miso tsukemen (海老味噌つけ麺) makes it heavier. A flavoured egg (味玉) is the topping to add if you add one.

fish-shinjuku.order_how: Table service, twenty-nine seats, walk-in. ⚠ It states that it is not taking online reservations, and the only booking channel it names is a phone one — so treat this as walk-in only; evening walk-ins are seated on dated reports. Cards, Suica and QR are all accepted. It closes between three and five, so this is a lunch or an evening meal, not a mid-afternoon one.
fish-shinjuku.order: Three-curry combo — keema and a mixed-bean curry are fixed, and the third is one you choose at the counter; chicken is the plain one. All three arrive on one plate with rice and a spread of pickles and sides.
fish-shinjuku.order_jp: 3種コンボを ひとつ、カレーは チキンで お願いします
fish-shinjuku.order_romaji: Sanshu konbo o hitotsu, karē wa chikin de onegai shimasu
fish-shinjuku.order_why: The combination plate is the house's own format rather than a sampler laid on for tourists — it is what the shop this kitchen continues was doing in Roppongi's Ark Hills for about thirty years, and the name, the recipes and the Indian head chef all came across with it when it reopened here. The three are meant to be eaten against each other and against the sides, and the spicing is built to be distinctive without being punishing.
fish-shinjuku.order_backup: The third curry is chosen from six — chicken, extra-hot chicken, white fish, prawn, pork, and a weekly one. The two-curry combo (2種コンボ) is the same idea, smaller. ⚑ Take the three unless you want less: the only day this shop is on is the Takao one, whose lunch is onigiri carried up the mountain, so you will not be arriving full.

rokurinsha.order_how: 🔴 Ticket machine, pay first — cash and transport IC both work at it. Staff walk the head of the queue to the machine, so join the line first and buy when you are brought forward. The touch panel's main split is tsukemen versus chūka soba. ⚠ Before 10:00 the shop serves a morning-only menu and the regular bowls are not available; at dinner that does not apply.
rokurinsha.order: Tokusei tsukemen — very thick, wavy noodles served cold beside a dense, long-reduced pork-and-fish dipping broth, with the shop's own shredded pork and a marinated egg added.
rokurinsha.order_jp: 特製つけめんを ひとつ お願いします
rokurinsha.order_romaji: Tokusei tsukemen o hitotsu onegai shimasu
rokurinsha.order_why: This is the shop that made thick, heavily reduced tsukemen the Tokyo standard, and the tokusei is its own number-one seller — the plain tsukemen with shredded pork and a marinated egg already added.
rokurinsha.order_backup: Plain tsukemen (つけめん) is the same broth and noodles without the toppings. Chūka soba (中華そば) is the hot bowl instead of the dipping one — a pork-bone-and-soy ramen the shop's own menu calls hefty and punchy, so do not take it for the light option. ⚑ The noodles come chilled by default; if you would rather have them warm, atsumori (あつもり) is the word for it.

kawashige-kamakura.order_how: Table service, forty seats — eight at the counter and thirty-two at tables — and walk-in. ⚑ The thing that makes it work at five in the afternoon: it runs straight through from eleven to eight with no break, so there is no opening rush to arrive into, and the kitchen's last order is seven. 🔴 CASH ONLY — no cards. ⚑ Shirasu comes two ways and they are different dishes: nama (生, raw) and kama-age (釜揚げ, boiled). The raw one depends on that morning's catch and on the weather, so it is not always on; the boiled one always is.
kawashige-kamakura.order: Shirasu-don — Sagami Bay whitebait heaped over rice, the dish Kamakura is known for.
kawashige-kamakura.order_jp: しらす丼を ひとつ お願いします
kawashige-kamakura.order_why: The agriculture ministry lists nama-shirasu-don among Kanagawa's own regional dishes, and this shop takes its whitebait from Sagami Bay, which is the water in question. Late October falls inside the fishing season — 11 March to 31 December — and autumn is one of its two peaks, the autumn fish being the fatter of the two.
kawashige-kamakura.order_backup: The tempura bowls are what the house is actually built on — its own site files the large-prawn tendon (大海老天丼) and the house tendon (川茂天丼) among its proudest dishes, while it files the shirasu bowl under what Kamakura is famous for. Both are finished with the kaeshi handed down at its 1887 sister house. There is also an eel bowl (うな丼) and a mixed seafood bowl (海鮮丼).

tenshinan.order_how: Table service in a converted house beside Kenchō-ji, with a garden room. This is a sit-down lunch, not a queue-and-go.
tenshinan.order: Denshō kenchin-jiru — the root-vegetable and tofu soup of Kenchō-ji next door, which the shop cooks to a method the temple taught it directly. The menu name is denshō kenchō-jiru (伝承 建長汁), glossed as kenchin-jiru (けんちん汁); at ¥1,100 it arrives as a meal, with a small dish and two salt rice balls.
tenshinan.order_jp: 伝承けんちん汁を ひとつ お願いします
tenshinan.order_romaji: Denshō kenchin-jiru o hitotsu onegai shimasu
tenshinan.order_why: Kenchin-jiru is eaten all over Japan, and the agriculture ministry gives two accounts of where the name came from: a Chinese temple dish called kenchin, or the kenchō-jiru made at Kenchō-ji, which is the temple you will have just walked through. This shop stands at its gate and cooks the soup under the temple's own instruction, which is as close as either story gets to a kitchen.
tenshinan.order_backup: Kenchin soba (けんちん蕎麦) is a country buckwheat noodle in a kenchin-style broth, at the same price as the soup. The other house dish is a curry built on Kamakura vegetables and honey taken from hives at Kenchō-ji itself — it can be had alone or with the soup added. ⚠ The hot-tofu set is winter-only and the chilled medicinal soba is summer-only, so neither is on in late October.

honke-daiichi-asahi.order_how: Order at the table — staff take it, no ticket machine. Cards and QR are accepted. Thirty-one seats, no reservations, and a queue outside at almost any hour, because it opens at six in the morning and runs past midnight. ⚠ Closed Thursdays.
honke-daiichi-asahi.order: Rāmen — thin straight noodles in a pork-and-soy broth, buried under sliced chāshū and a heap of Kujō leek, the Kyoto green onion, with mung-bean sprouts in it.
honke-daiichi-asahi.order_jp: ラーメンを ひとつ お願いします
honke-daiichi-asahi.order_why: This is the Kyoto bowl in its original form — the company's own account puts the shop at the Takabashi corner since 1947, and the other shops trading under the Daiichi-Asahi name came out of this one. The broth looks heavy and drinks light; the pork is the point.
honke-daiichi-asahi.order_backup: Tokusei rāmen (特製ラーメン) is roughly double the whole bowl, noodles included — the menu prints it as the large size, and it carries about five slices of chāshū instead of the usual few. If you want the pork without the extra noodles, chāshū-men (チャーシューメン) is the bowl that does that. ⚠ It is a great deal of pork for a late dinner — order it only if you skipped lunch.

kaidashimen-kitada.order_how: Order at the counter; cards and QR are accepted. Only eleven seats, no reservations. ⚑ It runs straight through from seven in the morning to ten at night with no midday break, which is what makes it the fallback whenever a day lands back in Kyoto at an hour when nothing else is serving.
kaidashimen-kitada.order: Kai-dashi men — ramen in a clear shellfish broth: asari and hamaguri clams and scallops, simmered down. ⚑ Not a meat-free bowl, whatever the name suggests: the shop's ramen come topped with chāshū, and both pork and chicken appear on its board.
kaidashimen-kitada.order_jp: 貝だし麺を ひとつ お願いします
kaidashimen-kitada.order_romaji: Kai-dashi men o hitotsu onegai shimasu
kaidashimen-kitada.order_why: The whole shop exists for this one idea, and it is the reason it is a Hyakumeiten pick — a shellfish broth is light in a way a pork broth never is, which is how the shop can trade from seven in the morning to ten at night without a break. ⚑ That fifteen-hour day is why it holds four slots on this trip — on each of them you arrive in the early evening with hours of service still ahead of you, which is the property the other candidates did not have.
kaidashimen-kitada.order_backup: Hamaguri rā-men (蛤らぁ麺) is the shop's other headline bowl — the same idea narrowed onto clams alone. A small bowl of shellfish simmered in soy over rice (貝のしぐれ煮ご飯, from ¥200) is the side to add if the ramen alone is not dinner.

yamamoto-mambo.order_how: 🔴 CASH ONLY — no cards, no e-money, no QR. Cooked on the griddle in front of you and eaten off it, with about half the seats at the teppan. ⚠ Reservations are recorded as accepted on weekdays but not at weekends or on holidays — all three visits here are weekdays. Twenty-three seats in total.
yamamoto-mambo.order: Manbo-yaki — the house dish: a thin betayaki base with noodles folded in, layered rather than stirred together, nothing like the Osaka or Hiroshima versions. ⚑ The plain one carries one filling, chosen at the counter — meat, squid, or abura-kasu, the crisp rendered offal; it is the Special (スペシャル) that has all of them plus egg and spring onion.
yamamoto-mambo.order_jp: まんぼ焼きを ひとつ お願いします
yamamoto-mambo.order_why: The shop has been open since 1948, and manbo-yaki is the dish it has built its name on — an evolved betayaki, Kyoto's own answer to okonomiyaki, which most people outside the city do not know exists. Where the name came from is not settled: the two accounts on offer are a customer groaning the word manbo at the taste, and the shape of the manbō, the sunfish. Ordering the plain betayaki here is ordering the thing without the reason for it.
yamamoto-mambo.order_backup: Beta-yaki (ベタ焼き) is the same base without the noodles piled in — lighter, and the better order if the day already had a big lunch.

arata.order_how: 🔴 CASH ONLY — no cards, no e-money, no QR. Teppan cooking, fifty seats, reservations accepted. ⚠ Evenings only, from five, and closed Sundays.
arata.order: Arata okonomi — the house build in the manbo-yaki style, layered rather than stirred: a thin base, cabbage and konjac, spring onion and fish powder, and agi, the beef jaw meat that gives it its bite. ⚑ It comes with noodles and without, under two names and about ¥300 apart; the noodle one is the version this describes, so say soba when you order if that is what you want.
arata.order_jp: あらたお好みを ひとつ お願いします
arata.order_romaji: Arata okonomi o hitotsu onegai shimasu
arata.order_why: Agi is what separates this from every other okonomiyaki on the trip — a cut most places will not bother with, slow enough to render that it turns the whole thing savoury. The shop has taken a Hyakumeiten place repeatedly on the strength of it.
arata.order_backup: Plain beta-yaki (ベタ焼き) without the agi is the milder order. If you would rather not eat another pancake, the griddle dishes stand on their own: agi grilled with salt (あぎ塩焼き), or tetchan-yaki (てっちゃん焼き), the offal one.

moritaya-kyoto-isetan.order_how: Proper table service on the 11th floor of the Isetan above Kyoto Station, with the city and its eastern hills through the window. 🔴 CASH OR CARD ONLY — the restaurant's own page states that electronic money and QR payment are not accepted, so an IC-only wallet fails here. ⚑ Walk in after 19:00: the floor's own rush is 18:00 to 19:00, last entry and last order are both 21:00, and a later sitting is the one with no line. ⚠ Lunch pricing stops at 16:00.
moritaya-kyoto-isetan.order: Sukiyaki — kuroge wagyū cooked at the table in an iron pan with sugar and soy, then dipped in raw beaten egg.
moritaya-kyoto-isetan.order_jp: すき焼きを ひとつ お願いします
moritaya-kyoto-isetan.order_why: Morita-ya opened in 1869 as Kyoto's first beef shop, and has run its own cattle farm at Wachi in Funai, north-west of the city, since 1981 — so the beef and the restaurant are the same business, which is the whole reason to eat sukiyaki here rather than anywhere cheaper. The set arrives as a sequence: an appetiser, the beef, vegetables and egg, then rice, red-miso soup, pickles and a dessert.
moritaya-kyoto-isetan.order_backup: Shabu-shabu is the same beef swirled through hot stock instead of simmered in soy — lighter and less sweet, and the order if the sugar-and-soy version sounds like too much after the day you have had. ⚑ Both of the evenings this shop is on are Kyoto in late autumn, so the sukiyaki is the seasonally obvious one. There is also an oil-yaki (オイル焼き), the same beef seared on the iron plate, and a separate steak course beside it.

wakakusa-curry.order_how: Order at the table; cards, Suica and QR are all accepted. Twenty-six seats, no reservations. ⚑ Aigake (あいがけ) is an item on the menu rather than a favour to ask for: you pick two of the four sauces — Wakakusa, mild, brown and chicken — and they come side by side on one plate, which is the way to try the house curry without giving up a second one.
wakakusa-curry.order: Wakakusa curry — the house bowl: spinach, tomato and other vegetables with chicken, spiced hard and thickened by the vegetables and the spices themselves rather than by a roux.
wakakusa-curry.order_jp: 若草カレーを ひとつ お願いします
wakakusa-curry.order_romaji: Wakakusa karē o hitotsu onegai shimasu
wakakusa-curry.order_why: The shop is named after this curry and it is the one that earned its Curry WEST Hyakumeiten place — dense and spice-forward rather than sweet. What the shop claims for it is that nothing thickens it but the vegetables and the spices: no flour roux, which is what most Japanese curry is built on. It sits about five minutes' walk from the Kintetsu station in a covered shopping street.
wakakusa-curry.order_backup: The chicken curry is creamy with coconut milk and mild, though not the mildest thing here — that is the Yamato-beef mild curry (大和牛マイルドカレー), a sweet roux the shop says a small child can eat, and the order if the day has been long. Lamb brown curry (ラムブラウンカレー) is the other end: slow-simmered lamb, and the hottest of the four. ⚑ If you cannot choose, aigake is its own order and puts two of them on one plate.

kamameshi-shizuka-koen.order_how: Table and tatami seating, forty-three seats, cards and QR accepted, no reservations. 🔴 Each pot is cooked from raw after you order — the shop cooks them one at a time over a direct flame — and diners consistently report about twenty minutes before it reaches the table. This is not a quick lunch, and that is the trade for the crisp scorched crust at the bottom. ⚠ The times the shop publishes are LAST ORDERS rather than closing times. The queue is a peak-lunch thing: about half an hour in the first hour of service on a weekday, longer at a weekend, and gone by mid-afternoon — which is the hour this shop is on the day for.
kamameshi-shizuka-koen.order: Nara nanashu kamameshi — rice cooked to order in its own iron pot under a crowd of toppings — prawn, crab, conger eel, chicken, burdock, carrot, shiitake and bamboo shoot among them — the nanashu (七種) in the name means plenty, not a count of seven.
kamameshi-shizuka-koen.order_jp: 奈良七種釜めしを ひとつ お願いします
kamameshi-shizuka-koen.order_romaji: Nara nanashu kamameshi o hitotsu onegai shimasu
kamameshi-shizuka-koen.order_why: It is the shop's most popular pot, from a house that has been cooking kamameshi in Nara for more than sixty years, and it stands directly opposite the Nara National Museum, so it is the natural lunch on a museum day. Scrape the bottom of the pot — the scorched layer, okoge, is the part people come back for.
kamameshi-shizuka-koen.order_backup: The single-ingredient pots are lighter and cheaper than the loaded one and cook in the same time — young chicken, prawn, crab, or the one with shimeji mushrooms and mountain vegetables. ⚑ A matsutake pot runs as the autumn special in limited numbers each day, but matsutake season is roughly September to October and the 31st is its far end — so treat that one as neither certain to be there nor priced with the rest: ask, rather than plan on it.

icchan-honten.order_how: 🔴 CASH ONLY — no cards, no IC, no QR. A small room of counter, griddle-side and table seats, and dine-in reservations are not available at all, so it is walk-in by construction. ⚑ You are asked one question when you order — soba or udon in the pancake, or neither. Say soba; that is the Hiroshima default.
icchan-honten.order: Niku-tama soba — the standard Hiroshima build: a thin crêpe, a mountain of cabbage, pork belly, fried noodles and an egg, pressed together on the griddle.
icchan-honten.order_jp: 肉玉そばを ひとつ お願いします
icchan-honten.order_romaji: Niku-tama soba o hitotsu onegai shimasu
icchan-honten.order_why: Hiroshima okonomiyaki is layered, not mixed — that is the whole difference from Osaka — and niku-tama soba is the base every shop is judged on. This one holds a Tabelog Hyakumeiten place three times over, in 2019, 2024 and 2025. ⚑ Its Michelin banner reads six years running; the two guides it names are Hiroshima 2013 and Hiroshima–Ehime 2018, so the Bib Gourmand itself is at best eight years old. The owner is the second generation, cooking under his own name after taking over his father's shop.
icchan-honten.order_backup: The toppings go on the left side of the order — spring onion, squid tempura (イカ天), prawn, cheese, squid, garlic or mochi, most of them ¥300–350. Squid tempura is the local one. Ask for udon instead of soba if you want it softer, or for no noodles at all.

okonomiyaki-masaru.order_how: Cards are NOT accepted; QR payment is. Twenty seats, all of them at the counter around the iron plate — there are no tables, so you eat where it is cooked. ⚠ It does take reservations, unusually for an okonomiyaki shop, but the only channel on record for them is a telephone one — so plan on walking in, and go at the open rather than late. It runs lunch and then again from the evening.
okonomiyaki-masaru.order: Niku-tama soba — the layered Hiroshima pancake with pork and noodles, finished on the plate in front of you.
okonomiyaki-masaru.order_jp: 肉玉そばを ひとつ お願いします
okonomiyaki-masaru.order_romaji: Niku-tama soba o hitotsu onegai shimasu
okonomiyaki-masaru.order_why: This is the base bowl of the local style and the fair comparison against the other okonomiyaki on the trip. ⚑ The shop is also a teppanyaki counter and prices higher than a plain okonomiyaki-ya, so the griddle dishes are a real part of what you are paying for rather than a sideline.
okonomiyaki-masaru.order_backup: Order a teppanyaki dish alongside rather than instead — the griddle is the reason this place costs more than its neighbours, and there are about twenty of them. ⚠ Ask at the counter for toppings rather than expecting a printed list: squid tempura (イカ天) is the one to look for, as it is anywhere in the city.

kunimatsu-ekie.order_how: ⚠ Credit cards are NOT accepted, but Suica and nanaco are. Counter seats only, inside the ekie complex at Hiroshima Station, so it is reachable without leaving the building. No reservations. ⚑ Ask for soy on the Musashibō half when you order — Kunimatsu's half is sesame only, and that difference is the whole reason for this order.
kunimatsu-ekie.order: Half-and-half — one bowl split between the two shops' versions of shiru-nashi tantanmen, Hiroshima's soupless dandan noodles, with a soft egg and rice.
kunimatsu-ekie.order_jp: ハーフ＆ハーフを ひとつ お願いします
kunimatsu-ekie.order_romaji: Hāfu ando hāfu o hitotsu onegai shimasu
kunimatsu-ekie.order_why: This counter is a collaboration between two of the city's best-known shiru-nashi tantanmen shops, and the half-and-half exists so you can eat both side by side. 🔴 The comparison is not automatic: Kunimatsu makes only a sesame bowl, while Musashibō will do sesame or soy — so the soy is something to ask for, and without it both halves can arrive sesame. Ordering a single bowl here gives up the only reason this branch exists.
kunimatsu-ekie.order_backup: Either shop's bowl on its own if you would rather not compare. ⚑ Each shop puts its own Sichuan pepper on the table, alongside the chilli oil, extra sauce and vinegar — the dish is meant to be adjusted, and stirring it thoroughly before the first mouthful is the local instruction. ⚑ Rice and the soft egg come with the set; cancel the rice and a second egg replaces it.

yakigaki-no-hayashi.order_how: Cards and QR accepted, e-money not. Eighty-six seats across tables and tatami, ten minutes up the Omotesandō shopping street from the pier. Reservations are not being taken at present. 🔴 Last order is 16:30 — half an hour before the close, so the door time is not the ordering time.
yakigaki-no-hayashi.order: Both of them — yaki-gaki, oysters cooked in the closed shell so they steam in their own liquor, and anago-meshi, conger eel over rice. ⚑ This shop does both of the island's dishes under one roof, so the day needs no second stop after 535 metres of stone stairs.
yakigaki-no-hayashi.order_jp: 焼がきを ひとつ お願いします
yakigaki-no-hayashi.order_why: The shop opened in 1948 and calls itself the origin house of grilled oysters, the first to have served them to the public — its own claim, on its own site, rather than an established fact. What the shop states as fact is the oyster: it buys from Jigozen and takes only the three-year ones.
yakigaki-no-hayashi.order_backup: The Itsukushima set (いつくしま定食) puts raw oysters, fried oysters and oyster rice on one tray — ¥3,000 with two raw oysters, ¥3,850 with four, and ¥650 more swaps the oyster rice for anago-meshi. It is the order if you want the oyster side of the menu rather than one of each. ⚑ There are also udon, soba, tonkatsu and fried-prawn sets, if neither island dish appeals by the time you sit down.

kakiya-miyajima.order_how: Cards and QR accepted. A hundred and ten seats over two floors, no reservations, and it runs straight through from 10:00 to 18:00 rather than shutting mid-afternoon. ⚠ It takes no fixed closing day but irregular closures do occur, and it may shut early once the day's oysters are gone. Look for the large white lantern on the Omotesandō.
kakiya-miyajima.order: Kakiya set — the house tray, ¥2,900: two grilled oysters, fried oysters, oyster rice, oysters in oil and an oyster miso soup.
kakiya-miyajima.order_jp: 牡蠣屋定食を ひとつ お願いします
kakiya-miyajima.order_romaji: Kakiya teishoku o hitotsu onegai shimasu
kakiya-miyajima.order_why: The set is how this shop shows what it does, which is oysters cooked five ways on one tray rather than one way well. ⚑ It grills them too, so the difference from the charcoal house up the street is breadth rather than method — this is the order if you want to understand the ingredient, and it does not cost you the island's dish to take it.
kakiya-miyajima.order_backup: Grilled oysters are sold from the front of the shop if you only want a couple standing up. ⚠ The two channels disagree on the unit: the shop's own menu prices them at ¥750 for the pair, its Tabelog listing at ¥330 each — carry the higher figure and do not count on being sold just one. The oysters in oil (牡蠣のオイル漬け) are jarred and travel; the shop's own site sells them through its online store.

tonkatsu-hasegawa-ryogoku.order_how: Cards and QR accepted, e-money not. Forty seats with a tatami room, two minutes from Ryōgoku station's east exit, on Yokozuna Yokochō behind a red noren. ⚠ It takes dinner reservations — never lunch — and stops once the evening is full, so as a walk-in go early in the service rather than late.
tonkatsu-hasegawa-ryogoku.order: Toku-rōsu katsu — the premium loin cutlet, Hirata Bokujō pork, fried in fresh panko.
tonkatsu-hasegawa-ryogoku.order_jp: 特ロースかつ定食を ひとつ お願いします
tonkatsu-hasegawa-ryogoku.order_romaji: Toku-rōsu katsu teishoku o hitotsu onegai shimasu
tonkatsu-hasegawa-ryogoku.order_why: This is the shop's own headline cut, and the pork is Hirata Bokujō's Bark sangen-ton — one named farm rather than a grade. ⚑ It is served with salt and wasabi rather than drowned in sauce — try a corner with salt alone before reaching for the bottle.
tonkatsu-hasegawa-ryogoku.order_backup: The fillet cutlet (ヒレかつ) is the leaner order. ⚑ Ryōgoku is sumo country and the obvious thing to eat here is chanko — this is the deliberate alternative to it, on the day that already has chanko at lunch.

kyoto-yamaroku.order_how: Order at the table; cards and QR accepted, e-money not. Twenty-one seats in the basement of the Isetan attached to Kyoto Station, so it is reachable without going outside. No reservations, and it queues at midday. ⚠ It runs two services with the middle of the afternoon shut: lunch 11:00 to 15:00, then dinner 16:00 to 20:00.
kyoto-yamaroku.order: Saikyō-yaki set — fish cured in sweet white Kyoto miso and grilled, with small seasonal side dishes, rice, miso soup and pickles.
kyoto-yamaroku.order_jp: 西京焼き定食を ひとつ お願いします
kyoto-yamaroku.order_romaji: Saikyō-yaki teishoku o hitotsu onegai shimasu
kyoto-yamaroku.order_why: The parent company has been curing fish in saikyō miso for over ninety years and this is its first restaurant — you are eating the product at the source rather than a restaurant's version of it. The miso draws water out of the fish and sweetens it, so it grills to something denser than plain fish. Pick the sablefish (gindara): it is a standing item on the menu rather than a daily special, and it is the one that goes soft rather than firm.
kyoto-yamaroku.order_backup: The fish is a choice, not a lottery — sablefish, salmon, Spanish mackerel and mackerel are all named on the menu, and there is a pork version beside them. ⚑ The small side dishes change with the season and are half the reason the set is worth having over a single grilled fish.

ginjo-ramen-kubota.order_how: 🔴 CASH ONLY — no cards, no e-money, no QR. Ten seats, counter only, no reservations. It runs a lunch service and then a separate evening one, so it is shut through the middle of the afternoon.
ginjo-ramen-kubota.order: Ginjō miso tsukemen — thick noodles dipped into a broth of three misos, Shinshū miso with gochujang and tenmenjan, wok-fried with pork mince, fish powder and the shop's own chilli oil.
ginjo-ramen-kubota.order_jp: 吟醸味噌つけ麺を ひとつ お願いします
ginjo-ramen-kubota.order_romaji: Ginjō miso tsukemen o hitotsu onegai shimasu
ginjo-ramen-kubota.order_why: Miso tsukemen is unusual anywhere — a Ramen WEST Hyakumeiten pick, and the chilli oil and fish powder make it sharper and hotter than the soy-based dipping broths elsewhere on this trip. ⚑ The ginjō in the name is not sake: the word means carefully chosen ingredients and slow brewing, and is said of miso and soy as much as of drink. Ordering the plain ramen here is ordering the thing it is not known for.
ginjo-ramen-kubota.order_backup: Ginjō shōyu rāmen (吟醸醤油らーめん) is the orthodox soy bowl and the lighter meal of the two.

ami-ryogoku.order_how: Cards, Suica and QR all accepted. A hundred and twenty seats across tables, tatami and sunken hearths, reservations taken, and it runs continuously from 11:00 to midnight. ⚑ The pot is cooked at your table on a portable burner, so allow time. Lunch chanko sets are a fraction of the evening price.
ami-ryogoku.order: Chanko-nabe — the stew sumo stables cook for their wrestlers, simmered at the table with chicken, seafood and vegetables.
ami-ryogoku.order_jp: ちゃんこ鍋を ひとつ お願いします
ami-ryogoku.order_why: Chanko is stable food rather than restaurant food, and eating it a few streets from the Kokugikan is the point of doing it in Ryōgoku at all. ⚠ The shop's own page says only that its recipe was handed down from a sumo stable; the Isegahama stable is named in listing copy, not by the shop. The chicken-based version is the traditional one — a chicken stands on two legs, and a wrestler down on four has lost, so stables kept four-footed meat out of the pot. ⚑ That is a superstition the stables have largely dropped since the 1960s; it survives mainly as a pre-tournament and new-year dish.
ami-ryogoku.order_backup: The seafood chanko is the lighter pot. ⚑ At the end, ask for rice or noodles to be cooked in what is left of the broth — that is how the stable finishes it, and it is where most of the flavour has ended up.

chanko-kirishima-edonoren.order_how: Cards, Suica and QR accepted. Eighty-eight seats inside the Edo NOREN hall directly outside Ryōgoku station's west exit — the building with a full-size sumo ring in its atrium. Reservations taken. Cooked at the table.
chanko-kirishima-edonoren.order: Kirishima chanko — the Michinoku stable's own recipe, a clear chicken-based pot finished at your table.
chanko-kirishima-edonoren.order_jp: ちゃんこ鍋を ひとつ お願いします
chanko-kirishima-edonoren.order_why: The restaurant belongs to the former ōzeki Kirishima, and its own page says the pot is his stable's recipe rather than a general-purpose one; the ceremonial apron he wore as a wrestler hangs in the room. ⚑ The Michinoku stable itself no longer exists — he reached the sumo association's retirement age of 65 in April 2024, the stable closed and its wrestlers moved to Otowayama. The building is worth the walk on its own: Edo NOREN keeps a full-size dohyō on its ground floor.
chanko-kirishima-edonoren.order_backup: Kirishima teba-saki, the shop's own fried chicken wings, are ¥700 and are what the menu puts beside the pot. ⚑ Ask for the rice or noodles at the end, cooked in the remaining broth.

hiraso-horyuji.order_how: Table service, at the gate of Hōryū-ji — half shop, half restaurant, with a café counter as well. You can eat in and buy boxes to take away from the same building.
hiraso-horyuji.order: Nara lunch (奈良ランチ) — four kinds of kakinoha-zushi, a bowl of Miwa sōmen, a seasonal dish, pickles and a dessert. From October to June the sōmen comes hot, as nyūmen. ⚑ Ask for it by name: that is what distinguishes it from the plainer trays.
hiraso-horyuji.order_jp: 奈良ランチを ひとつ お願いします
hiraso-horyuji.order_romaji: Nara ranchi o hitotsu onegai shimasu
hiraso-horyuji.order_why: Kakinoha-zushi is cured fish pressed onto vinegared rice and wrapped in a persimmon leaf — a mountain food that let sea fish keep in a Yoshino with no coast. It was a household dish there before Hiraso, founded in 1861, turned it into something sold; the house styles itself sōhonke on that ground rather than on having invented it. The set is the way to eat it as a meal rather than as a souvenir box.
hiraso-horyuji.order_backup: The plain kakinoha-zushi set — three mackerel, three salmon, with a clear soup — is the unadorned version. ⚑ Unwrap the leaf and leave it: the tannin in it keeps the fish and takes the smell off, but it is not eaten.

matsumotoya-horyuji.order_how: Table service, no reservations needed — a coach-tour dining hall at the Hōryū-ji gate with a quieter dining room and café alongside it, so a table is not the problem. ⚠ Carry cash: its own listing takes JCB and nothing else, and no channel of the shop's mentions Visa, Mastercard, e-money or QR. ⚠ It publishes no weekly closing day but states that it closes irregularly, so an open day cannot be asserted in advance.
matsumotoya-horyuji.order: Kaki udon — the shop's own invention: persimmon worked into the udon dough, served hot or cold.
matsumotoya-horyuji.order_jp: 柿うどんを ひとつ お願いします
matsumotoya-horyuji.order_romaji: Kaki udon o hitotsu onegai shimasu
matsumotoya-horyuji.order_why: Hōryū-ji and persimmons are joined by the most famous haiku in Japan about eating one — Shiki's line about biting a persimmon as the temple bell rings — and the shop opens its own pages with it, having built a handful of persimmon dishes on the association. The noodles are its own recipe, and it sells packs of them to take home.
matsumotoya-horyuji.order_backup: Kaki zaru udon is the same noodles served cold, if the walk down from the temple has been warm. ⚑ The persimmon soft-serve afterwards is the same joke told a second way.

katsui-yamanobe.order_how: Proper table service in a yōshoku restaurant on the Yamanobe-no-michi — a sit-down meal in the middle of a walking day, so budget the time rather than expecting a counter.
katsui-yamanobe.order: Hamburg steak set — a ground-beef patty with rice, soup and sides.
katsui-yamanobe.order_jp: ハンバーグステーキ定食を ひとつ お願いします
katsui-yamanobe.order_romaji: Hanbāgu sutēki teishoku o hitotsu onegai shimasu
katsui-yamanobe.order_why: Yōshoku is Japan's own century-old reworking of European cooking, and the hamburg steak is its central dish — this kitchen also does kuroge wagyū and beef stew at several times the price, which tells you the beef is taken seriously. The set is the affordable end of a serious menu.
katsui-yamanobe.order_backup: The prawn-fry set (エビフライ定食) is the other set at the same price for three prawns, more for five. The grilled wagyū set is the step up if the day deserves it.

picton-yanagimoto.order_how: A small canteen inside Yanagimoto station, run by the same people as the yōshoku restaurant up the road. Simple and quick — which is the entire reason it is the backup here rather than a destination. ⚠ It shuts on Mondays and Tuesdays.
picton-yanagimoto.order: Whatever the day's set is — this is a station canteen, and the board by the counter is the menu.
picton-yanagimoto.order_jp: 本日のおすすめを ひとつ お願いします
picton-yanagimoto.order_romaji: Honjitsu no osusume o hitotsu onegai shimasu
picton-yanagimoto.order_why: It exists so the Yamanobe-no-michi walk has a hot meal waiting at the end of it — the value is that it is at the station and open, not that it is remarkable. ⚑ It is one of four places the same operator runs, Katsui up the road among them.
picton-yanagimoto.order_backup: Ask what is quickest if the train time is tight — that phrase above simply asks for today's recommendation, which is the safest order in any canteen.

denbe-kibune.order_how: Seated strictly first-come — it accepts no reservations of any kind and seats people in the order they arrive. 🔴 Cash: its listings state that cards, electronic money and QR are all refused, so do not arrive without notes. ⚠ It shuts when the soba runs out rather than at a set hour, and the opening time is given as 11:00 to 11:30 depending on the day — so this is a stop to make when you reach it, not one to come back to. ⛔ The riverbed platforms everyone photographs are a summer arrangement — in November you are eating indoors, and that is normal, not a disappointment.
denbe-kibune.order: Soba — since 2022 it is the whole menu, and the line-up changes with the season. Read the day's list at the counter rather than arriving with a dish in mind.
denbe-kibune.order_jp: おそばを ひとつ お願いします
denbe-kibune.order_why: Kibune is a narrow cold valley of shrine and river, and its restaurants are mostly expensive kaiseki aimed at the summer riverbed trade. This is the one that stays plain and reasonable year-round, and a hot bowl is the right thing in a valley that is genuinely cold in November.
denbe-kibune.order_backup: There is no second thing to order here — the menu is soba and the day's list is short. If what you wanted has gone, the next door is the café a minute up the lane rather than another bowl at this counter.

kibune-club.order_how: A café rather than a restaurant — a wooden building in the valley serving hot drinks and light meals. Quieter than the soba houses and the better option if what you want is to sit down and get warm. ⚑ Order the food, not the tea: you are here because the noodle house down the lane could not seat you, so this is lunch. The food menu runs October to May only, which is why it is available at all in November, and it is four dishes at ¥1,300 to ¥2,200 — not café money.
kibune-club.order: Kyō-yuba gohan, about ¥1,550 — sheets of tofu skin with wheat gluten and fish cake in broth over rice, with red miso soup, a small dish and pickles.
kibune-club.order_jp: 京湯葉御飯を ひとつ お願いします
kibune-club.order_romaji: Kyō-yuba gohan o hitotsu onegai shimasu
kibune-club.order_why: Yuba is skimmed off simmering soy milk and is one of the few genuinely Kyoto things on a plate. It arrives hot, and unlike the kamameshi it is not cooked from raw, so it comes out without a wait.
kibune-club.order_backup: The house dish is wild boar, three ways: inoshishi kamameshi ¥2,200, a boar and egg-yolk rice bowl ¥1,700, or boar curry ¥1,300 in a limited daily run. ⚠ The kamameshi is the one to think twice about — it is cooked from raw in its own pot and takes about twenty minutes, on a stop you reached because you were already running late, with last order at 16:00. Matcha and a cake set from ¥1,280 if you only want to sit down. ⚑ Only one listing carries this food menu, so read all four prices as approximate.

suzuriishitei.order_how: 🔴 Cash — its listing states that cards, electronic money and QR are all refused, and the day's gates are cash too. A mountain teahouse standing on the stone steps themselves, about half way between the Takao bridge and Jingo-ji's gate. Order at the counter and sit on the benches out front.
suzuriishitei.order: Yuba soba — buckwheat noodles in hot broth with sheets of tofu skin, which is a Kyoto ingredient rather than a garnish.
suzuriishitei.order_jp: 湯葉そばを ひとつ お願いします
suzuriishitei.order_romaji: Yuba soba o hitotsu onegai shimasu
suzuriishitei.order_why: It stands half way up the Jingo-ji steps, beside the inkstone rock it is named for, so you pass its door climbing and again coming down — which is exactly where you will want to sit. A hot bowl is the right thing at that moment in November. Yuba is skimmed off simmering soy milk and is one of the few genuinely Kyoto things on a plate.
suzuriishitei.order_backup: ⚑ The thing the shop is actually famous for is momiji mochi, a maple-leaf rice cake, taken with matcha — order that instead if you only want to stop for ten minutes rather than eat.

takao-chaya.order_how: A mountain teahouse up on the Jingo-ji steps, not down by the river. Order at the counter, and it will put the food up to take away if the benches are full. 🔴 Cards and electronic money are both refused; a QR app is the only cashless channel it takes, so carry cash unless you have one running.
takao-chaya.order: Momiji udon with yuzu (柚子入もみじうどん) — house-made udon in hot broth. The soba version is the same price.
takao-chaya.order_jp: もみじうどんを ひとつ お願いします
takao-chaya.order_romaji: Momiji udon o hitotsu onegai shimasu
takao-chaya.order_why: The udon and the rice cakes are both made in the building, and firm-textured noodles are the thing the house claims for itself. A hot bowl is the right order half way down a cold gorge in November.
takao-chaya.order_backup: All three things it sells are momiji dishes. The two-colour soba — mugwort and plum — with seasonal rice is the fuller meal; matcha with the house momiji-mochi is the ten-minute stop rather than a lunch.

yakko-yoshino.order_how: Table and tatami seating, sixty-three of them, no reservations, directly in front of Kinpusen-ji. 🔴 Its two channels name two different card brands and neither names Visa or Mastercard, so treat this one as cash.
yakko-yoshino.order: Kakinoha-zushi — salt-cured mackerel or salmon pressed on vinegared rice and wrapped in a persimmon leaf.
yakko-yoshino.order_jp: 柿の葉寿司を ひとつ お願いします
yakko-yoshino.order_why: The fish is cured in salt and only the rice is vinegared, and the persimmon leaf is there to keep it and to scent it — unwrap it and leave it, it is not eaten. ⚑ This is the second time the trip meets the dish: Hōryū-ji's came from the 1861 house that turned it into a product, and this is the mountain-village version on the ridge it came off.
yakko-yoshino.order_backup: Kuzu udon — noodles in a broth thickened with Yoshino arrowroot until it turns glossy — is the local speciality and the warmer order on a ridge in November. ⚑ Order both: the sushi travels, the udon does not.

harukaze-yoshino.order_how: A plain eating house on the Yoshino ridge road, table service, and it takes cards — which the better-known house a few doors along cannot promise. ⚑ Not small either: 66 seats inside and 6 on a terrace, more than that neighbour has, so a queue there is not a queue here.
harukaze-yoshino.order: Kuzu udon — udon in a broth thickened with Yoshino arrowroot starch, which turns it glossy and holds the heat.
harukaze-yoshino.order_jp: 葛うどんを ひとつ お願いします
harukaze-yoshino.order_romaji: Kuzu udon o hitotsu onegai shimasu
harukaze-yoshino.order_why: Yoshino kuzu is the arrowroot the whole region is known for, and thickening a hot broth with it is the local way to eat it savoury rather than as a sweet. A thickened broth holds its heat longer than a clear one, which is what you want at the top of a cold ridge walk.
harukaze-yoshino.order_backup: Kakinoha-zushi, the persimmon-leaf sushi, is the other Yoshino thing and is sold here too.

tsukumo-udon.order_how: Order at the counter; every card, Suica and the QR apps are all accepted. Thirty-five seats — 21 at the counter, 14 at tables — on the second basement level of Kyoto Station, at the east exit. ⚑ 07:00 to 22:00 with last orders at 21:30, no closing day, which is what makes it the answer when a day has run long.
tsukumo-udon.order: Keiran curry udon (鶏卵カレーうどん) — the bowl the shop leads with: curry broth over its own udon with egg through it.
tsukumo-udon.order_jp: 鶏卵カレーうどんを ひとつ お願いします
tsukumo-udon.order_romaji: Keiran karē udon o hitotsu onegai shimasu
tsukumo-udon.order_why: The broth under the curry is built slowly and cold from Kujūkushima iriko and Rishiri kombu, then finished with a second iriko from the Inland Sea, and the udon is cut in the shop.
tsukumo-udon.order_backup: ⚑ If curry is the wrong thing at that hour, ask for the same bowl without it, keiran udon (鶏卵うどん) — that is the egg in the plain iriko broth and is the way to taste the dashi itself. ⚠ Only the curry version is named on the shop's listings, so the plain one is an ask rather than a certainty. The tempura zaru udon, chicken or vegetable, are the cold alternatives, and there is a beer set after 17:00 — a glass with chicken, sweet potato and chikuwa tempura.

ekibenya-matsuri.order_how: ⛔ Not a restaurant — a shop. Take a box off the shelf, queue at the till, pay with Suica or a card. Nothing is spoken and nothing is cooked to order. ⚑ Ask for chopsticks if none are handed over: 「お箸をください」 (o-hashi o kudasai).
ekibenya-matsuri.order: Whichever box you want — around a hundred and fifty kinds, from all over the country, restocked through the day.
ekibenya-matsuri.order_jp: これを ひとつ お願いします
ekibenya-matsuri.order_why: About a hundred and fifty kinds, so the point is the choice and not a particular box — regional bento from lines that terminate far from Tokyo are brought in and restocked through the day. ⚑ Buy something from where you are going or where you have been; that is what the format is for.
ekibenya-matsuri.order_backup: ⚑ The phrase above is for pointing at something behind glass. If a box can be heated the staff will ask you — the question is atatamemasu ka (温めますか), shall I warm it, and yes is hai (はい).

ekibenya-odori.order_how: ⛔ Not a restaurant — a shop, right beside its neighbour on the same passage: carry on past the stairs down to platforms 7–8 and it faces the Tōkaidō–Sanyō Shinkansen central transfer gate. Take a box, pay at the till, cards and Suica accepted. ⚑ It stocks the ten best-selling boxes rather than the full range.
ekibenya-odori.order: Whichever box you want — a selected range rather than the full national spread.
ekibenya-odori.order_jp: これを ひとつ お願いします
ekibenya-odori.order_why: It exists as the edited version of the counter beside it: the operator stocks it with the ten best-selling boxes rather than the whole national range. ⚑ That makes it the stop to take when the first one is busy and the train is soon — which is exactly the situation it is listed for.
ekibenya-odori.order_backup: ⚑ Whatever is bought, buy it BEFORE passing through the Shinkansen transfer gate — both counters sit outside it.

yumehyakusen-ekie.order_how: ⛔ Not a restaurant — a souvenir and bento hall on the second floor of ekie at Hiroshima Station. Take a box, pay at the till. ⚑ It is OUTSIDE the ticket gates, so buy before you go through; once you are in, it is behind you.
yumehyakusen-ekie.order: Anago-meshi — conger eel, grilled and laid over rice cooked in its stock. The box from Ueno at Miyajimaguchi is the one to look for.
yumehyakusen-ekie.order_jp: あなごめしを ひとつ お願いします
yumehyakusen-ekie.order_why: Anago-meshi is the dish of this stretch of coast, and Ueno has been selling this box since 1901, when it began as the station bento for the Miyajima line — you will have spent the previous day on the island it is named after. ⚠ Deliveries come in from Miyajimaguchi and can sell out, so this is a preference, not a plan.
yumehyakusen-ekie.order_backup: If the anago box has gone, any of the other counters in the hall will do — the day has about ninety minutes of slack here, so nothing about this stop is rushed.

ethiopia-akihabara.order_how: Table service inside Atre at Akihabara station, reachable without going outside. 🔴 You are asked two things. First, how hot — the scale runs 0 to 70, where 0 is 中辛 and 3 is 辛口, so say 「3ばい」 (san-bai); anything past 10 is a decision, not a preference. Second, whether you want a drink, which comes alongside a curry rather than instead of one — the order line below declines it, so drop the last clause if you want one. ⚑ Steamed potatoes come free with the curry and can be refilled.
ethiopia-akihabara.order: Chicken curry (チキンカリー) — a thin, twelve-spice curry with vegetables and pulses cooked down into it.
ethiopia-akihabara.order_jp: チキンカリーを 3ばいで お願いします。ドリンクは大丈夫です
ethiopia-akihabara.order_romaji: Chikin karī o san-bai de onegai shimasu. Dorinku wa daijōbu desu
ethiopia-akihabara.order_why: The house has been making this since 1988 in Jinbōchō and it is one of the reference points for Japanese-style spice curry. The curry sauce is built on twelve spices with vegetables and beans cooked to nothing, so it tastes deep rather than merely hot even at the low numbers.
ethiopia-akihabara.order_backup: Beef, greens, prawn and bean curries sit on the same heat scale, but the three bean ones (bean, chicken-and-bean, greens-and-bean) start at three times and cannot be ordered milder — the order line above already clears that floor. ⚠ There is no pork on the spiced line at all; this branch runs European-style roux curries beside it, and neither the chain nor the branch publishes this board, so read the board itself for anything past those. ⚠ The scale is real: the shop will go past 70 on request and there is no reason to find out.

fukokuen-horyuji.order_how: Table service in a hundred-and-thirty-year-old house, with an English menu — the one place on this street where you are not ordering blind. Cards, e-money and QR are all accepted. ⚑ Lunch is served 11:00 to 14:00 only; the room stays open to 16:00 for cake and coffee after the kitchen has stopped. ⚠ Thirty-nine seats, and the shop's own booking slots skip the twelve o'clock hour entirely — that is the hour it fills. If it is full, put your name down and sit in the garden, or walk on: the sushi house is 400 m west and on your way to the station either way.
fukokuen-horyuji.order: Ikaruga tatsuta-age lunch (斑鳩名物竜田揚げランチ) — chicken marinated in shio-kōji and fried, with the house's own wholemeal Miwa sōmen in broth, Yoshino shiitake in it, and small seasonal dishes.
fukokuen-horyuji.order_jp: 竜田揚げランチを ひとつ お願いします
fukokuen-horyuji.order_romaji: Tatsuta-age ranchi o hitotsu onegai shimasu
fukokuen-horyuji.order_why: Tatsuta-age is Ikaruga's own dish — soy-marinated fried chicken named for the Tatsuta river whose autumn maples the speckled coating is said to resemble — and the town has built a promotion around it. This house mills its own wholemeal version of Miwa sōmen with a Miwa producer, so the plate pairs the town's dish with the noodle of the village tomorrow's walk ends in. The building was a Meiji judicial official's retirement house and then, from 1954, the town's wedding hall.
fukokuen-horyuji.order_backup: You can ask for ordinary Miwa sōmen instead of the wholemeal noodle. ⚑ The other sets are a pork cold-shabu salad and a smaller one-dish lunch; the beef roast lunch is the only thing here that must be booked a day ahead, so it is not an option on the day.

meals.time_hint: Arrival night — no clock on it. The first rung walks straight in; the better bowl below it has a line

restaurants.note: Inside Atre Akihabara 1 at the station, 150 m from the hotel and reachable without going outside. Open to 22:30, last order 22:00, so there is no hour at which you are too late. Table service, no reservations, 26 seats. ⚠ How busy it gets in the evening is not something any source measures — but with last order at 22:00 you can walk away from a line and come back. Cards and IC. ⚠ It publishes no closing day of its own and follows Atre's calendar.

The better bowl of the two — but the way in is a line, about ten people and 15–20 minutes on a normal evening. It is a minute from the station on the same walk, so you can look at the door and decide. ⚠ Dinner is 18:00 to 21:30, and one channel prints 21:00 instead. If the line is there, Atre is 150 m on and Kamayoshi ten minutes the other way.

meals.time_hint: On the walk home, in Akihabara

restaurants.note: Last order 20:00, an hour before the close. Six minutes from the hotel. ⚠ The shop keeps no channel of its own — no site, no social account — so its hours cannot be confirmed before you fly; keep the backup live.

🔴 THE BRANCH THAT WORKS AT ANY HOUR, and the one to take if you are off the mountain later than planned. Table service, 26 seats, open until 22:30 with last order at 22:00, cards and IC accepted — and it is in Atre at Akihabara station, 150 m from the hotel and on the walk home, so it costs no detour at all. ⇒ You do not have to decide before you board: if you reach Shinjuku after about half four, stay on the train.

About ten minutes from the Keiō concourse. ⇒ Use it only if you are eating at 17:30 or later and will take a queue you cannot size in advance.

Directly opposite the Shinkansen central transfer gate — still on the outside of it, like its neighbour.

restaurants.note: Inside the Tenri City Trail Center, on the road itself just past Chōgaku-ji. ⚠ The menu changes at 14:00 and set meals stop at 15:30, well before the 16:30 close. ⚑ A third option sits behind both of these: a convenience-store picnic bought at Tenri before you start, through the arcade the walk begins in.
About twenty minutes on from the Trail Center, and it doubles as the bail-out: Yanagimoto is the walk's first station, so cutting the day short and eating are the same move.

meals.time_hint: At base — back at Kyoto Station around 17:30–18:30

restaurants.note: Five to eight minutes from the hotel, on the west side of the station. ⚑ Eleven seats and no reservations, and the line here has never been counted — hour-long waits are reported, but by nobody who put a date or a number on one. The shop trades from seven in the morning to ten at night with no midday break, last order 21:30, so a 17:30–18:30 arrival has three to four hours in hand. ⇒ If there is a line, walk away and come back — nothing here asks you to stand in one. ⚠ It closes on irregular days that it publishes nowhere readable.

Last order 22:15, and ten minutes on foot from the Hachijō exit on the south side of the station — 700 m, measured 2026-08-22 after the pin was corrected. ⚑ Reservations here are not merely accepted but recommended — a walk-in can be turned away on a busy night.

meals.time_hint: Nara city, after Kasuga-taisha and on the way down towards Naramachi

restaurants.note: 🔴 There is no lunch deadline here, whichever Shōsō-in slot you hold: last entry 19:25, last order 19:30, no midday break. In the Mochiidono covered arcade, ten to twelve minutes west of the museum — and everything is plated to order, so nothing sells out. ⚑ Two minutes further on is Menya K (麺屋K), an eleven-seat Ramen WEST Hyakumeiten counter that shuts when it sells out: if the arcade shows no line, take it as an upgrade. restaurants.note: In Nara Park itself, by the museum — the only one of the day's three that needs no walk west into the arcades. 🔴 16:00 is the last order, not the close. It is the cover for the day running late rather than early: the half-hour queue reported around 11:20 is a weekday figure and a peak Saturday runs longer than that, but by 15:00 it is gone either way. ⚠ It declares one irregular closure a month. If that closure lands on the 31st, the primary answers at any hour and the only cost is the walk west into the arcade.

meals.time_hint: At base — back at Kyoto Station around 21:15, off the 20:28 Kintetsu express from Nara

restaurants.note: Five minutes from the hotel, and it runs to one in the morning — nothing tonight can arrive too late for it. ⚑ The Nara alternative is still open: if you are out of the Shōsō-in by 19:45 rather than 20:00, Tori-soba Zagin at Kintetsu Nara (105 m from the station on the Konishi-dōri arcade, Saturday 11:00 to 21:00, last order 20:30, walk-in only, no closing day) becomes comfortable and is worth taking, with four later trains behind it. Decide on the night.

Last order 22:15, and ten minutes on foot from the Hachijō exit — 700 m, measured 2026-08-22 — which is the side the Kintetsu from Nara arrives on. ⚠ On the Kintetsu you are at the station ~21:15, so the walk lands you ~21:25 with an hour in hand. ⛔ Cash only while the primary takes cards — carry notes for it. ⚑ Reservations here are recommended, not merely accepted.

meals.time_hint: On the Kibune lane, coming down off the ridge crossing from Kurama

restaurants.note: ⚠ It shuts when its soba runs out rather than at a fixed hour, and a peak-autumn Sunday is this lane's busiest day. ⚑ Two options sit behind it.
